## Your route {#route}

**What does a fitted regression model claim, and which evidence could weaken it?**

We use the familiar `airquality` data to fit ozone on temperature, compare its
training error with a simple baseline, then add wind and investigate what the
model missed. Reading a coefficient correctly matters as much as obtaining it.
A fluent explanation, including an LLM-generated explanation, needs evidence
for each sentence.

[Before you start](#before-start) · [Words used here](#words) · [Setup](#setup) ·
[Meeting 1](#meeting-one) · [Meeting 2](#meeting-two) · [AI audit](#ai-audit) ·
[Practice and resources](#practice).

::: {.callout-tip}
## A first 30-minute session

Choose a stopping point within about 30 minutes and resume later. This is an
untested stopping budget, not a completion promise.

1. Check prerequisites and setup; resolve access first if blocked.
2. Try the row-accounting prediction and read the modeling-table check.
3. Read the temperature coefficient and mean-baseline comparison; state what
   they describe and which observations they use.
4. Inspect the diagnostic flag explanation, then choose the next Core step.

Read displayed results when jumping ahead; run the code in order when returning

selected lab/exercises share the **90–120-minute ordinary-week practice budget**.

### Before you start {#before-start}

You should be able to open and run an R script, read a pipe, identify a table's
row meaning, handle `NA` explicitly and understand a function with a checked
input/output contract. Review [Week 11](https://lnajman.github.io/math346/companion/week-11.html)
for contracts and [Week 12](https://lnajman.github.io/math346/companion/week-12.html)
for complete result records. No regression command syntax is assumed.

Slides provide lecture flow, this chapter explains and checks it, and the
selected lab/exercises provide practice. Week 13 fits and diagnoses a few
declared models; repeated modeling across groups/formulas belongs to Week 14.

::: {.callout-note #words}
## Words used in this chapter

| Word or pattern | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| **Response / predictor** | The variable being modeled / a variable used to describe its average relationship. |
| **Formula** | In `y ~ x`, model response `y` using predictor `x`; reversing them changes the question. |
| **Complete case** | A row with observed values for every variable required by the declared model. |
| **Coefficient / slope / intercept** | Numbers defining the fitted line; the slope is change per predictor unit, the intercept its value at predictor zero. |
| **Fitted value / residual** | The model's estimate on a modeling row / observed response minus that estimate. |
| **Baseline** | A simple comparison rule: predict the same training mean for every row. |
| **Training RMSE** | Square root of mean squared prediction errors on the rows used for fitting, in response units. |
| **R-squared** | The fraction of response variation accounted for by the fitted relationship on its modeling rows. |
| **Standardized residual** | A residual scaled to make unusually large discrepancies easier to screen. |
| **Cook's distance** | A measure of how much a row affects the fitted model; it is not a probability of error. |
| **Conditional coefficient** | A slope interpreted while holding the other included predictor fixed. |
| **Extrapolation / validation** | Predict beyond observed conditions / assess a declared model on data not used to fit it. |
:::

### Read / Explain / Check / Interpret

Read the variables and formula; explain a prediction; check a specific claim;
interpret with units, population and limitations. Think first; write a private
comment only where requested—see the [prediction guide](https://lnajman.github.io/math346/companion/how-to-use.html#read-explain-check-interpret).

## Meeting 1 · State what the fitted line describes {#meeting-one}

**Slide cues:** “Modeling Contract”, “Observational Question”, “Build The Modeling Table”
and “Account For Exclusions”.

### Choose the rows before fitting {#rows}

One source row is one recorded day in New York from May through September 1973.
The response is ozone in ppb; temperature is in degrees Fahrenheit and wind is
in miles per hour. We ask about an **observational association**, not what an
intervention changing temperature would cause.

**Predict in a private comment first:** `airquality` has 153 rows and 37 missing
`Ozone` values. Temperature and wind are complete. How many complete rows can
both models use? Does keeping every retained row once show that the omitted
days are representative of the others?

<details>
<summary>Compare the row reasoning</summary>

Both models use the same 116 rows; 37 are excluded because ozone is missing.
Row accounting records the selection but does not establish representativeness.
**If your answer differed,** you may have confused missing cells with missing
rows or treated a consistent count as evidence about omitted days.

</details>

For Core 1/2, state the contract and attempt the table in your starter before
running this check. `observation_id` is created **before** filtering so it still
points to the original source row.

```{r}
#| label: modeling-population
library(dplyr)
model_rows <- airquality |>
  transmute(observation_id = row_number(), ozone_ppb = Ozone,
            temperature_f = Temp, wind_mph = Wind) |>
  filter(complete.cases(ozone_ppb, temperature_f, wind_mph))
stopifnot(
  nrow(airquality) == 153,
  sum(is.na(airquality$Ozone)) == 37,
  !anyNA(airquality$Temp), !anyNA(airquality$Wind),
  nrow(model_rows) == 116, !anyNA(model_rows),
  n_distinct(model_rows$observation_id) == 116
)
data.frame(original = nrow(airquality), retained = nrow(model_rows),
           excluded = nrow(airquality) - nrow(model_rows))
```

A silent `stopifnot` means its conditions passed; an error identifies the failed
condition. Check the named input before changing a failed assertion.

### Read the formula, then the implementation {#simple-model}

**Slide cues:** “Plot Before Fitting”, “Read The Formula”, “Fitted Equation”,
“Interpret The Slope”, “Intercept Warning”, “Fitted Plus Residual”, “Preserve Row Alignment”
and “Check The Alignment”.

For Core 3, read `ozone_ppb ~ temperature_f` as “model mean ozone using
temperature.” `~` declares a formula; it is not an assignment. `lm` estimates a
line from the declared modeling rows. `coef` returns its intercept and slope.
Reversing the formula models temperature instead and changes both units and
question.

For Core 4/6, write one slope sentence and name the comparison baseline in your
starter before opening the complete reference. Trace the formula, then the
fitted/residual columns, then each argument to `rmse`.

<details>
<summary>Reference version · Simple model and training baseline</summary>

```{r}
#| label: simple-reference
# MATH 346 - possible worked solution
# Compare only after attempting the starter; other correct implementations are possible.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

model_data <- airquality |>
  transmute(
    observation_id = row_number(),
    ozone_ppb = Ozone,
    temperature_f = Temp
  ) |>
  filter(complete.cases(ozone_ppb, temperature_f))

stopifnot(
  nrow(model_data) == 116,
  identical(range(model_data$temperature_f), c(57L, 97L)),
  !anyNA(model_data)
)

relationship_plot <- ggplot(
  model_data,
  aes(x = temperature_f, y = ozone_ppb)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Temperature (degrees F)",
    y = "Ozone (ppb)"
  )

relationship_build <- ggplot_build(relationship_plot)
stopifnot(nrow(relationship_build$data[[1]]) == nrow(model_data))

ozone_fit <- lm(ozone_ppb ~ temperature_f, data = model_data)

model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(
    fitted_ozone_ppb = fitted(ozone_fit),
    residual_ppb = residuals(ozone_fit)
  )

rmse <- function(observed, predicted) {
  stopifnot(
    is.numeric(observed),
    is.numeric(predicted),
    length(observed) == length(predicted),
    !anyNA(observed),
    !anyNA(predicted)
  )

  sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2))
}

baseline_prediction <- mean(model_data$ozone_ppb)
baseline_rmse <- rmse(
  model_data$ozone_ppb,
  rep(baseline_prediction, nrow(model_data))
)
model_rmse <- rmse(
  model_data$ozone_ppb,
  model_data$fitted_ozone_ppb
)

coefficients <- coef(ozone_fit)
model_r_squared <- summary(ozone_fit)$r.squared

stopifnot(
  abs(coefficients[["(Intercept)"]] - (-146.995491)) < 1e-6,
  abs(coefficients[["temperature_f"]] - 2.428703) < 1e-6,
  abs(model_r_squared - 0.4877072) < 1e-6,
  abs(mean(model_data$residual_ppb)) < 1e-12,
  model_rmse < baseline_rmse
)

prediction_inputs <- tibble(temperature_f = c(70, 80, 90))
prediction_outputs <- prediction_inputs |>
  mutate(predicted_ozone_ppb = predict(ozone_fit, newdata = prediction_inputs))

stopifnot(
  nrow(prediction_outputs) == 3,
  all(prediction_outputs$temperature_f >= min(model_data$temperature_f)),
  all(prediction_outputs$temperature_f <= max(model_data$temperature_f))
)

model_summary <- tibble(
  quantity = c(
    "observations used",
    "temperature slope (ppb per degree F)",
    "R-squared",
    "baseline training RMSE (ppb)",
    "model training RMSE (ppb)"
  ),
  value = c(
    nrow(model_data),
    coefficients[["temperature_f"]],
    model_r_squared,
    baseline_rmse,
    model_rmse
  )
)

print(model_summary)
print(prediction_outputs)
cat("Week 13 simple-linear-model checks passed.\n")
```

</details>

The printed summary reports a slope near **2.428703 ppb per degree F**, an
R-squared near **0.487707**, and training RMSEs near **32.8 ppb** for the mean
baseline and **23.5 ppb** for the line. The reference prediction inputs 70, 80
and 90 F lie inside the observed 57–97 F range; making these predictions is not
a new-data accuracy test because no observed responses are evaluated for them.

**Predict · Think first:** the intercept is about -147.0. Is it an observed
negative ozone value? What does a positive residual mean?

<details>
<summary>Compare coefficients and residuals</summary>

The intercept is the fitted line at 0 F, outside these modeling temperatures;
it is not a negative measurement in the table. A positive residual means the
observed ozone exceeds its fitted value. **If your answer differed,** distinguish
the fitted line from source measurements and read residual as observed minus
fitted, not the reverse.

The slope describes an estimated change in **mean ozone associated with** a
one-degree difference within these conditions. It does not describe every day's
change or establish causation.

</details>

The reference checks how many points reached the scatter layer. View it and
check row alignment independently. These checks use the reference object names;
run the modeling-table check and reference above first. If your completed
starter uses other names, adapt the names in these checks:

```{r}
#| label: simple-evidence
print(relationship_plot)
stopifnot(
  identical(model_data$observation_id, model_rows$observation_id),
  length(fitted(ozone_fit)) == nrow(model_data),
  length(residuals(ozone_fit)) == nrow(model_data),
  max(abs(model_data$ozone_ppb -
          (model_data$fitted_ozone_ppb + model_data$residual_ppb))) < 1e-12,
  abs(rmse(c(0, 2), c(1, 1)) - 1) < 1e-12
)
```

For the last check, the two prediction errors are -1 and 1. Squaring gives 1
and 1; their mean and its square root are 1. That known answer checks the RMSE
calculation independently. The reconstruction identity checks row alignment;
neither check proves the model describes the pattern well.

### Compare like with like {#baseline}

**Slide cues:** “Mean Baseline”, “Fair Training Comparison”, “Training Is Not Validation”,
“R-Squared” and “R-Squared Is Not”.

The mean baseline repeats one number for every training row. The line changes
its fitted value with temperature. Both RMSEs must use the **same response,
same 116 rows and same units**. Lower RMSE means smaller squared discrepancies
on that comparison, not “more observations predicted exactly.”

**Predict in a private comment first:** after seeing 23.5 versus 32.8 ppb, can
you say the line predicts a new summer's days well? Does R-squared about 0.488
mean 48.8% of these days were predicted correctly?

<details>
<summary>Compare what the metrics support</summary>

The line fits these training rows better than the mean baseline. No new days
were assessed. R-squared describes response variation accounted for by the
fitted relationship on these rows; it is not a classification accuracy rate.
**If your answer differed,** you may have mistaken fitting evidence for
validation evidence or read “fraction of variation” as “fraction of days.”

</details>

**Individual in-class exit, final five minutes:** name one supported claim and
one unsupported claim about the fitted model. Follow the announced classroom
route.

**Self-check (no submission):** a report compares a model's RMSE on 116 complete
rows with a baseline computed on a different subset of 100 rows. Both numbers
are in ppb. What must be fixed before interpreting their difference?

<details>
<summary>Compare the Meeting 1 self-check</summary>

Recompute both predictions and RMSEs on one declared set of rows with the same
response. Equal units alone do not make different populations comparable.
Then label the comparison training or new-data evaluation according to where
the model was fitted and assessed.

</details>

## Meeting 2 · Investigate what remains {#meeting-two}

**Slide cues:** “Meeting 2 Question”, “Residual Plot”, “Look For Structure”,
“Standardized Residuals”, “Cook's Distance”, “Diagnostic Flags Ask Questions”,
“Add Wind”, “Conditional Coefficients” and “Same-Row Comparison”.

### Rebuild the declared additive model {#diagnostics}

Resuming here? The complete reference and following diagnostic check can run
together in a fresh session; no saved Meeting 1 model object is needed.

The second reference builds a table containing ozone, temperature **and wind**,
then fits both formulas on it. Because wind has no missing values here, its
116 source IDs agree with the earlier simple-model table. In another dataset,
adding a predictor could change the complete-case population; check IDs, not
just counts, before comparing fits.

`temperature_f + wind_mph` includes both predictors. A temperature slope now
compares fitted means at the **same wind speed**; the wind slope holds
temperature fixed. These remain adjusted associations. The formula adds no
interaction term, so its temperature slope does not change with wind.

For Core 8, locate the additive formula, the diagnostic columns and the flag
conditions in your starter before opening the reference. Trace the model fit,
then its residuals, Cook's distances and plot in that order.

<details>
<summary>Reference version · Additive model and diagnostic flags</summary>

```{r}
#| label: diagnostic-reference
# MATH 346 - possible worked solution
# Compare only after attempting the starter; other correct implementations are possible.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

model_data <- airquality |>
  transmute(
    observation_id = row_number(),
    ozone_ppb = Ozone,
    temperature_f = Temp,
    wind_mph = Wind
  ) |>
  filter(complete.cases(ozone_ppb, temperature_f, wind_mph))

stopifnot(nrow(model_data) == 116, !anyNA(model_data))

simple_fit <- lm(
  ozone_ppb ~ temperature_f,
  data = model_data
)
additive_fit <- lm(
  ozone_ppb ~ temperature_f + wind_mph,
  data = model_data
)

model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(
    simple_prediction = predict(simple_fit),
    additive_prediction = predict(additive_fit),
    additive_residual = residuals(additive_fit),
    standardized_residual = rstandard(additive_fit),
    cooks_distance = cooks.distance(additive_fit)
  )

rmse <- function(observed, predicted) {
  stopifnot(length(observed) == length(predicted), !anyNA(observed), !anyNA(predicted))
  sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2))
}

baseline_prediction <- mean(model_data$ozone_ppb)
comparison <- tibble(
  model = c("mean baseline", "temperature", "temperature + wind"),
  training_rmse_ppb = c(
    rmse(model_data$ozone_ppb, rep(baseline_prediction, nrow(model_data))),
    rmse(model_data$ozone_ppb, model_data$simple_prediction),
    rmse(model_data$ozone_ppb, model_data$additive_prediction)
  ),
  r_squared = c(
    NA_real_,
    summary(simple_fit)$r.squared,
    summary(additive_fit)$r.squared
  )
)

residual_plot <- ggplot(
  model_data,
  aes(x = additive_prediction, y = additive_residual)
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65) +
  labs(
    x = "Fitted ozone (ppb)",
    y = "Residual (ppb)"
  )

residual_build <- ggplot_build(residual_plot)
stopifnot(nrow(residual_build$data[[2]]) == nrow(model_data))

influence_threshold <- 4 / nrow(model_data)
flagged <- model_data |>
  filter(
    abs(standardized_residual) > 2 |
      cooks_distance > influence_threshold
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(cooks_distance))

additive_coefficients <- coef(additive_fit)

stopifnot(
  abs(additive_coefficients[["temperature_f"]] - 1.840179) < 1e-6,
  abs(additive_coefficients[["wind_mph"]] - (-3.055491)) < 1e-6,
  abs(summary(additive_fit)$r.squared - 0.5687097) < 1e-6,
  abs(mean(model_data$additive_residual)) < 1e-12,
  comparison$training_rmse_ppb[[3]] < comparison$training_rmse_ppb[[2]],
  comparison$training_rmse_ppb[[2]] < comparison$training_rmse_ppb[[1]],
  sum(model_data$cooks_distance > influence_threshold) == 7,
  sum(abs(model_data$standardized_residual) > 2) == 4,
  flagged$observation_id[[1]] == 117
)

print(comparison)
print(flagged)
cat("Week 13 diagnostic flags are prompts for investigation, not automatic deletion rules.\n")
cat("Week 13 model-diagnostic checks passed.\n")
```

</details>

These checks use the object names from the reference above. Run that reference
first; if your completed starter uses other names, adapt them in these checks.

```{r}
#| label: diagnostic-evidence
print(residual_plot)
expected_model_ids <- which(complete.cases(airquality[c("Ozone", "Temp", "Wind")]))
stopifnot(
  identical(model_data$observation_id, expected_model_ids),
  max(abs(model_data$ozone_ppb -
          (model_data$additive_prediction + model_data$additive_residual))) < 1e-12
)
data.frame(
  model = "temperature + wind",
  large_standardized_residuals = sum(abs(model_data$standardized_residual) > 2),
  cooks_flags = sum(model_data$cooks_distance > influence_threshold),
  either_flag = nrow(flagged)
)
```

Read the residual plot as fitted ozone horizontally and **observed minus
fitted ozone** vertically, both in ppb. The dashed horizontal line is zero.
Points above it were underpredicted. Look for bends, changes in vertical spread,
clusters and isolated points. A near-zero mean residual can coexist with those
patterns; with an intercept it is a fitted-model algebraic property, not a
complete diagnostic pass. Some fitted values are negative here: these are model
estimates, not negative recorded ozone measurements. That is a limitation to
inspect in this unconstrained linear model.

The additive temperature slope is about **1.840179 ppb per degree F** and the
wind slope about **-3.055491 ppb per mph**. These answer a different, conditional
question from the simple model's 2.428703. Its training RMSE is about **21.6 ppb**,
with R-squared about **0.568710**. Added predictors can improve training fit;
new-data evidence is still missing.

### Flags invite questions, not automatic deletion

For this **additive model**, four residuals exceed 2 in absolute standardized
units and seven Cook's distances exceed `4/116`, about 0.0345. `abs` checks
both negative and positive residuals. Cook's distance measures influence, not
whether a measurement is false. The script's `|` selects a row meeting **either**
condition; a row meeting both still appears once.

**Predict · Think first:** must the combined flag table contain 4 + 7 = 11 rows?
Does crossing the Cook's threshold justify removing a row immediately?

<details>
<summary>Compare the flag logic</summary>

The groups can overlap, so add their counts only after accounting for overlap.
Read `either_flag` above and compare the source IDs in `flagged`. No threshold
alone justifies deletion. **If your answer differed,** you may have counted
memberships rather than distinct rows, or treated a screening rule as proof
that a value is wrong.

</details>

The reference sorts flagged rows by Cook's distance; the first is original
**observation 117**, not “the 117th retained row” (there are only 116 retained
rows). Use `observation_id` to recover the source day. Ask whether its measurement
is valid, whether unusual weather/context is real, and how much the fitted
conclusion depends on it. Do not remove it just to improve a metric. Repeating
whole modeling workflows is next week's topic.

## Guided audit · A fluent explanation is a set of claims {#ai-audit}

**Slide cues:** “AI Claim Audit” and “Do Not Declare A Winner Yet”.

Use this section selectively for **Guided 10**; the full AI-review lab is not
an additional required lab. The candidate is supplied locally; no external AI
call is involved.

> “Increasing temperature by one degree causes ozone to rise by 2.43 ppb.
> The intercept predicts ozone at 0 F. An R-squared of 0.49 means 49% of
> observations are predicted correctly. The low training error proves the model
> will predict new days well, and the residuals show no unusual observations.”

Before revealing the audit, choose evidence for each claim:

| Candidate claim | Evidence to inspect first |
|---|---|
| “causes” | How the data were collected; a fitted number alone cannot settle this |
| meaningful prediction at 0 F | Observed temperature range |
| percent predicted correctly | What R-squared measures |
| good new-day predictions | Which rows trained the model and which rows were evaluated |
| no unusual observations | Residual/influence output for the specified model |

**Predict in a private comment first:** select one sentence, name the exact
output or design fact you would check, then write a defensible replacement.
A grammatically correct sentence or a passing R script is not enough.

<details>
<summary>Compare the evidence and run the supplied audit</summary>

```{r}
#| label: ai-reference
library(dplyr)

model_data <- airquality |>
  transmute(
    observation_id = row_number(),
    ozone_ppb = Ozone,
    temperature_f = Temp
  ) |>
  filter(complete.cases(ozone_ppb, temperature_f))

ozone_fit <- lm(ozone_ppb ~ temperature_f, data = model_data)

generated_interpretation <- paste(
  "Increasing temperature by one degree causes ozone to rise by",
  "2.43 ppb. The intercept predicts ozone at 0 F.",
  "An R-squared of 0.49 means 49% of observations are predicted correctly.",
  "The low training error proves the model will predict new days well,",
  "and the residuals show no unusual observations."
)

coefficients <- coef(ozone_fit)
r_squared <- summary(ozone_fit)$r.squared
standardized_residuals <- rstandard(ozone_fit)
cooks_distances <- cooks.distance(ozone_fit)

rmse <- function(observed, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2))
}

baseline_rmse <- rmse(
  model_data$ozone_ppb,
  rep(mean(model_data$ozone_ppb), nrow(model_data))
)
training_rmse <- rmse(model_data$ozone_ppb, predict(ozone_fit))

audit <- tibble(
  generated_claim = c(
    "temperature causes ozone to rise",
    "the intercept is a meaningful prediction at 0 F",
    "R-squared is the percentage predicted correctly",
    "training error proves performance on new days",
    "there are no unusual observations"
  ),
  verdict = rep("unsupported or incorrect", 5),
  evidence = c(
    "the fitted observational association does not establish causation",
    paste("observed temperatures range from", min(model_data$temperature_f),
          "to", max(model_data$temperature_f), "F"),
    "R-squared describes variation accounted for by the fitted model",
    "training predictions reuse the same observations used for fitting",
    paste(sum(abs(standardized_residuals) > 2),
          "standardized residuals exceed 2 in absolute value")
  )
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(model_data) == 116,
  abs(coefficients[["temperature_f"]] - 2.428703) < 1e-6,
  min(model_data$temperature_f) == 57,
  max(model_data$temperature_f) == 97,
  abs(r_squared - 0.4877072) < 1e-6,
  training_rmse < baseline_rmse,
  sum(abs(standardized_residuals) > 2) == 5,
  sum(cooks_distances > 4 / nrow(model_data)) == 5,
  nrow(audit) == 5
)

cat(generated_interpretation, "\n\n")
print(audit)
cat("Week 13 AI model-interpretation audit passed.\n")
```

The audit is for the **temperature-only model**: it has **five** large
standardized residuals and **five** Cook's flags. Earlier counts 4/7 belong to
the additive model; diagnostics depend on the model, not just the dataset.
The intercept sentence is algebraically correct; using that value as a meaningful
prediction for these conditions is the unsupported step. Qualify it with the
observed range rather than calling the definition itself false.

A defensible interpretation says: on these 116 observed days, temperature is
associated with mean ozone, with fitted slope about 2.43 ppb per degree F.
The intercept is algebraically the value at 0 F, but that is outside the
observed 57–97 F range. About 0.488 of response variation is accounted for on
these modeling rows. Training RMSE is lower than the mean baseline, with flagged
observations to investigate; no new-day performance was measured.

**If your answer differed,** you may have accepted the explanation's confidence
instead of identifying the model, units, design and evaluation rows behind it.
Read all code and claims you accept from an LLM and keep the checks required by
the [course AI policy](https://lnajman.github.io/math346/syllabus/ai-policy.html).
Never supply private student information or assessment keys to an external tool.

</details>

**Individual in-class exit, final five minutes:** “Write one supported model
claim, one unsupported claim, and one diagnostic that would change your
confidence.” Follow the announced classroom route.

**Self-check (no submission):** a large positive residual and a Cook's flag
occur for the same day. Explain what each measures and name a useful next
investigation without deciding the day is an error.

<details>
<summary>Compare the Meeting 2 self-check</summary>

The positive residual says observed ozone exceeded the fitted value; Cook's
distance concerns how much that row affects the fit. Inspect the original
source day, measurement validity and conditions, and ask whether the conclusion
depends strongly on it. Neither diagnostic establishes a data-entry mistake.

</details>
